parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of forming a partnership rather than continuing as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. more capital is available; partners bring different skills and ideas; work and responsibility are shared; losses are shared; cover during illness or holidays.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of forming a partnership rather than continuing as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. profits have to be shared; decisions take longer and partners may disagree; each partner is liable for the debts of the firm (unlimited liability); a partner is bound by the actions of the others.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four items that are usually included in a partnership agreement.
parts.answer: Any four: the ratio for sharing profits and losses; capital to be contributed by each partner; interest on capital (rate); interest on drawings (rate); partners' salaries; limits on drawings; procedure for admitting or retiring partners; how disputes are settled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a partnership appropriation account.
parts.answer: It shows how the profit for the year is shared between the partners: interest on capital, salaries, interest on drawings and the share of the residual profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: shows how profit is divided/appropriated. 1 mark: names at least two items.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Aziz and Bano share profits and losses in the ratio 3:2. Their profit for the year was $48,000. Interest on capital: Aziz $3,000, Bano $2,000. Bano receives a salary of $10,000. Interest on drawings: Aziz $500, Bano $300. What is Aziz's share of the residual profit?
A $20,280
B $19,800
C $28,800
D $13,520
parts.working: Residual profit = 48,000 + interest on drawings 800 − interest on capital 5,000 − salary 10,000 = 33800. Aziz's share = 3/5 × 33800 = 20280. B forgets to add interest on drawings; D is Bano's share.

practice.stem:
Hina and Omar are partners in a travel agency in Peshawar. Their partnership agreement provides for:
• interest on capital at 5% per annum (capitals: Hina $80,000, Omar $50,000)
• a salary for Omar of $12,000 per year
• interest on drawings: Hina $640, Omar $410
• residual profits and losses shared equally
The profit for the year ended 31 December was $64,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest on capital for each partner.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the residual profit and each partner's share of it.
parts.answer: Residual profit $47,050; Hina $23,525; Omar $23,525

practice.stem:
Lerato and Sipho are partners. On 1 January Lerato's current account had a credit balance of $3,200 and Sipho's had a debit balance of $850. For the year ended 31 December:
• interest on capital: Lerato $2,700, Sipho $1,800
• salary: Sipho $9,000
• share of residual profit: Lerato $15,600, Sipho $10,400
• drawings: Lerato $24,000, Sipho $18,500
• interest on drawings: Lerato $720, Sipho $480

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance on each partner's current account on 31 December. State whether each is a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: Lerato $3,220 debit; Sipho $1,370 credit

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a debit balance on a partner's current account shows.
parts.answer: The partner has withdrawn more (drawings and interest on drawings) than the total of his or her share of profit, interest and salary, so the partner owes this amount to the business.
parts.working: 1 mark: drawings exceed amounts credited. 1 mark: partner owes the firm/reduces the partner's equity.

practice.stem: Amina and Bashir share residual profits and losses in the ratio 2:1. The partnership agreement provides for interest on drawings at 10% per annum and a salary for Amina of $7,500 per year. No interest is allowed on capital. The financial year ends on 31 December. Amina withdrew $6,000 on 1 April and Bashir withdrew $8,000 on 1 October; there were no other drawings. The profit for the year was $39,100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest on drawings for each partner.
parts.answer: Amina $450; Bashir $200
parts.working: Amina: 6,000 × 10% × 9/12 = 450 (1). Bashir: 8,000 × 10% × 3/12 = 200 (1). Charging a full year loses the mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the residual profit.
parts.answer: Amina $21,500; Bashir $10,750

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a partnership agreement may charge interest on drawings.
parts.answer: To discourage partners from taking drawings early or in large amounts, which would reduce the cash available to the business.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader does not keep a full set of records. Her capital was $42,000 at the start of the year and $51,500 at the end. During the year her drawings were $12,000 and she introduced additional capital of $3,000. What was her profit for the year?
A $18,500
B $24,500
C $9,500
D $500
parts.working: Profit = closing capital + drawings − capital introduced − opening capital = 51,500 + 12,000 − 3,000 − 42,000 = 18500. B adds the capital introduced instead of deducting it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a statement of affairs.
parts.answer: A statement listing the assets and liabilities of a business on a particular date, used to calculate the owner's capital when full records are not kept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Guo Wei runs a phone repair stall. On 1 July his business had: equipment $9,400; inventory of spare parts $3,750; amounts owed by customers $2,180; cash $640; amounts owed to suppliers $1,960; loan from a relative $5,000; rent owing $300. Calculate his capital on 1 July.

practice.stem:
Nimmi does not keep a full set of double-entry records. For the year ended 31 March she has this information:
Trade receivables: 1 April $5,400; 31 March $6,100
Trade payables: 1 April $3,800; 31 March $4,250
Received from credit customers $47,300; discount allowed $900
Paid to suppliers $31,600; discount received $450
Cash sales $12,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the credit sales for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total revenue for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the credit purchases for the year.

practice.stem: Carlos sells sports goods and always earns a gross margin of 30% on revenue. For the year his revenue was $90,000, opening inventory was $7,200 and purchases were $61,500. He did not count his closing inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the closing inventory.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mark-up percentage that is equal to a gross margin of 30%. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: Mark-up = gross profit ÷ cost of sales = 30 ÷ 70 × 100 = 42.86%.

practice.stem:
On 20 April a fire destroyed most of the inventory of Mumtaz Crockery. The following information is available for the period from 1 January to 20 April:
Inventory at cost on 1 January $14,800
Purchases $39,600
Revenue $52,000
Mumtaz always uses a mark-up of 25% on cost. Undamaged inventory with a cost of $2,300 was saved.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales for the period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the inventory destroyed by the fire.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the gross margin percentage that is equal to a mark-up of 25%.

practice.stem: Daniyal owns a hardware shop but does not keep full records. On 1 January his business assets were $58,400 and liabilities $12,900. On 31 December assets were $71,250 and liabilities $15,600. During the year he took $1,200 cash each month for personal use and also took goods costing $950. In June he paid a legacy of $6,000 that he had received into the business bank account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Daniyal's capital on 1 January and on 31 December.
parts.answer: 1 January $45,500; 31 December $55,650

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of calculating profit in this way rather than preparing an income statement.
parts.answer: e.g. it shows only the total profit, not the revenue, gross profit or individual expenses, so the owner cannot see where costs can be controlled or calculate margins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by prime cost.
parts.answer: The total of the direct costs of production: direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses (such as royalties).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
State where each cost appears: in the prime cost section of the manufacturing account, in factory overheads, or in the income statement.
(i) wages of machine operators
(ii) rent of the factory
(iii) commission paid to salespeople
(iv) depreciation of factory machinery
(v) salaries of office staff
(vi) raw materials used
parts.answer: (i) prime cost (ii) factory overheads (iii) income statement (iv) factory overheads (v) income statement (vi) prime cost
parts.working: 1 mark for each two correct answers (6 correct = 3 marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by work in progress.
parts.answer: Goods that have been partly manufactured at the end of the period (started but not yet finished).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how opening and closing work in progress are used to calculate the cost of production.
parts.answer: Opening work in progress is added to (and closing work in progress deducted from) the total of prime cost and factory overheads.
parts.working: 1 mark opening added, 1 mark closing deducted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two reasons why a manufacturing business prepares a manufacturing account.
parts.answer: Any two: to calculate the cost of production of goods completed; to find the cost per unit; to control and compare factory costs; to help set selling prices; to decide whether to make or buy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A manufacturer provides the following information.
Inventory of raw materials: opening $4,200; closing $5,100
Purchases of raw materials $36,500
Carriage inwards on raw materials $800
Direct labour $28,000
Royalties $2,500
Factory rent $9,000
What is the prime cost?
A $66,900
B $66,100
C $64,400
D $68,700
parts.working: Raw materials consumed = 4,200 + 36,500 + 800 − 5,100 = 36400. Prime cost = 36400 + 28,000 + 2,500 = 66900. Factory rent is a factory overhead, not part of prime cost. B leaves out carriage inwards.

practice.stem:
Shahid Furniture makes tables. For the year ended 30 June:
Inventory of raw materials: 1 July $6,300; 30 June $7,450
Purchases of raw materials $48,700
Carriage inwards $1,150
Purchases returns $850
Direct wages $39,800
Indirect factory wages $8,600
Factory power $5,250
Depreciation of factory machinery $4,000
Work in progress: 1 July $3,100; 30 June $3,900

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of raw materials consumed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the prime cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the cost of production of completed goods.

practice.stem:
Ama Textiles shares some costs between the factory and the office. For the year ended 31 December:
Rent and rates $18,000 (three-quarters factory, one-quarter office)
Insurance $4,800 (two-thirds factory, one-third office)
Electricity $7,500 (60% factory, 40% office)
Indirect factory wages $11,200
Factory machinery cost $60,000; accumulated depreciation on 1 January $21,600. Machinery is depreciated at 20% per annum by the reducing balance method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation of factory machinery for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total factory overheads.
parts.working: Rent 13,500 + insurance 3,200 + electricity 4,500 + indirect wages 11,200 + depreciation 7680 = 40080. 1 mark each for the three shares, 1 for the total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total of these costs that will be charged in the income statement.

practice.stem: Rahul Plastics produced 12,000 buckets in the year at a cost of production of $128,400. Inventory of finished goods was $9,600 at the start of the year and $11,200 at the end. Revenue for the year was $165,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the cost of production per bucket.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why the closing inventory of finished goods is valued at cost and not at selling price.
parts.answer: Valuing at selling price would include a profit that has not yet been earned, because the goods have not been sold (realisation/prudence). Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit not yet realised/earned. 1 mark: prudence or lower of cost and NRV.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is meant by limited liability for the shareholders of a company?
A the company can only borrow a limited amount of money
B shareholders can lose only the amount they have invested in their shares
C shareholders receive a fixed dividend every year
D the company has a limited number of shareholders
parts.answer: B shareholders can lose only the amount they have invested in their shares
parts.working: With limited liability, shareholders' personal possessions cannot be used to pay the company's debts; the most they can lose is the amount paid for their shares. C describes a feature that ordinary shares do not have: ordinary dividends vary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two differences between ordinary shares and debentures.
parts.answer: Ordinary shareholders are owners of the company, while debenture holders are lenders (creditors). Ordinary shareholders receive dividends that vary with profit and are paid only if declared; debenture holders receive a fixed rate of interest that must be paid whether or not there is a profit. (Also: shareholders usually have voting rights; debentures are repayable on a fixed date.)
parts.working: Two differences × 2 marks (1 for each side of the comparison).

practice.stem:
On 1 January the equity of Indus Foods Ltd was: ordinary shares of $1 each $200,000; general reserve $30,000; retained earnings $47,500. During the year ended 31 December:
• 50,000 further ordinary shares of $1 each were issued at par for cash
• the profit for the year was $61,200
• $15,000 was transferred to the general reserve
• ordinary dividends of $24,000 were paid

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance on each of the following on 31 December: (i) ordinary share capital, (ii) general reserve, (iii) retained earnings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total equity on 31 December.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of the financial statement in which these movements are shown.
parts.answer: Statement of changes in equity

practice.stem: Kestrel Engineering Ltd has 6% debentures of $120,000, repayable in 2034. For the year ended 31 December the company's profit from operations was $84,600. Only $3,600 of debenture interest had been paid and recorded during the year. Retained earnings on 1 January were $52,300. During the year ordinary dividends of $30,000 were paid and $10,000 was transferred to the general reserve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the debenture interest to be charged in the income statement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.
parts.working: 84,600 − 7200 = 77400. (Deducting only the 3,600 paid loses the A mark.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings on 31 December.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State where each of the following appears in the statement of financial position: (i) the debentures, (ii) the unpaid debenture interest.
parts.answer: (i) non-current liabilities (ii) current liabilities (other payables/accruals) of $3,600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mariam owns a successful bakery as a sole trader. She plans to form a limited company and issue 60,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each at par. Calculate the amount the company would receive if all the shares were issued and fully paid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Mariam whether she should convert her business into a limited company. Justify your answer by giving two advantages and two disadvantages.
parts.answer: Advantages: limited liability protects her personal assets; more capital can be raised by selling shares; the company continues even if a shareholder dies or leaves. Disadvantages: she must share profits (dividends) and control with other shareholders; more legal formalities and costs; financial statements may have to be published, so there is less privacy. Recommendation, e.g. convert if she needs large amounts of capital for expansion; otherwise remain a sole trader.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks advantages, up to 2 marks disadvantages, 1 mark for a justified recommendation (only if both sides are given).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the financial statements of a club, the accumulated fund is equivalent to which item in the financial statements of a sole trader?
A capital
B profit for the year
C drawings
D bank balance
parts.answer: A capital
parts.working: The accumulated fund is the members' interest in the club: assets less liabilities, the same as a sole trader's capital. The surplus for the year (not the fund itself) corresponds to profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A tennis club received subscriptions of $8,400 during the year. This included $200 owing from the previous year and $600 paid in advance for next year. At the start of the year $300 had been paid in advance for this year. At the end of the year $450 was owing for this year. What is the subscriptions income for the year?
A $8,350
B $8,450
C $8,250
D $9,150
parts.working: 8,400 − 200 (last year's arrears) − 600 (next year) + 300 (paid last year for this year) + 450 (owing) = 8350. C ignores the opening balances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between a receipts and payments account and an income and expenditure account.
parts.answer: Any two: a receipts and payments account is a summary of the cash book, while an income and expenditure account is like an income statement; the receipts and payments account includes capital items, the income and expenditure account includes only revenue items; the income and expenditure account includes accruals, prepayments and depreciation, the receipts and payments account does not; the receipts and payments account ends with a cash/bank balance, the income and expenditure account with a surplus or deficit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Gulberg Chess Club had the following subscription balances: 1 January: in arrears $240, in advance $180. 31 December: in arrears $510. During the year $9,850 was received, which included the $240 arrears from last year and $360 for next year. Calculate the subscriptions income for the year.
parts.working: 9,850 − 240 − 360 + 180 + 510 = 9940. 1 mark for removing the two amounts not for this year, 1 for adding 180 and 510, 1 for the answer.

practice.stem:
The Riverside Hiking Society runs a small café for members. For the year ended 31 December:
Café takings $14,600; café purchases $8,900; café inventory 1 January $650, 31 December $820; café wages $3,100
Subscriptions income $12,400
Competition entry fees $1,350; competition prizes $980
Rent of clubhouse $6,000
Electricity paid $1,780; $160 was owing at 31 December (nothing owing at 1 January)
Depreciation of equipment $1,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit made by the café.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the surplus or deficit for the year.
parts.answer: Surplus of $6,100
parts.working: Income: 12,400 + café 2770 + net competition 370 = 15540 (2). Expenditure: 6,000 + electricity 1940 + 1,500 = 9440 (1). Surplus 6100 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of the surplus on the accumulated fund.
parts.answer: It increases the accumulated fund.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader provides this information: opening inventory $7,300; purchases $52,600; carriage inwards $900; purchases returns $1,400; closing inventory $8,100. What is the cost of sales?
A $51,300
B $50,400
C $54,100
D $49,500
parts.working: 7,300 + 52,600 + 900 − 1,400 − 8,100 = 51300. B leaves out carriage inwards, which is part of the cost of purchases; C adds the returns instead of deducting them.

practice.stem:
Jaya owns a gift shop. For the year ended 31 December: revenue $96,500; sales returns $1,500; inventory 1 January $8,000; purchases $61,000; inventory 31 December $9,500; wages paid $14,200; rent paid $7,200; discount received $350; equipment at cost $24,000.
Additional information:
• wages of $600 were owing at 31 December
• rent of $600 had been paid in advance at 31 December
• equipment is depreciated at 10% per annum on cost (straight-line method)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.

practice.stem:
The following information relates to Ewan's shop on 31 December, after the income statement had been prepared:
Premises $90,000
Fixtures at cost $18,000; accumulated depreciation $7,200
Inventory $11,300
Trade receivables $8,400; provision for doubtful debts $420
Insurance prepaid $250
Bank $3,170
Trade payables $6,950
Wages accrued $380
Loan repayable in 2031 $25,000
Capital 1 January $83,000; profit for the year $17,670; drawings $9,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total of the non-current assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total of the current assets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the working capital.
parts.working: Current liabilities = 6,950 + 380 = 7330 (1). 22700 − 7330 = 15370 (1). The loan is non-current and is not included.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate Ewan's capital on 31 December and show that it equals the net assets of the business.
parts.answer: Capital $91,170; net assets $91,170

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A credit sale of $350 to Raza Traders was correctly entered in the sales journal but was posted to the account of Rehman Traders. What type of error is this?
A commission
B principle
C original entry
D omission
parts.answer: A commission
parts.working: The amount is posted to the wrong account of the same class (the wrong customer's account), which is an error of commission. It is not an error of principle, because both accounts are personal accounts of credit customers.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of error in each case.
(i) A payment of $260 for electricity was not recorded in the books at all.
(ii) The purchase of a delivery van was debited to the motor expenses account.
(iii) A credit sale of $1,470 was entered in the sales journal as $1,740 and posted from there.
(iv) A cheque paid to a supplier was debited to the bank account and credited to the supplier's account.
parts.answer: (i) omission (ii) principle (iii) original entry (iv) complete reversal

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of error that are not revealed by a trial balance.
parts.answer: Any two of: omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal, compensating errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a suspense account may be opened when a trial balance is prepared.
parts.answer: When the trial balance totals do not agree, the difference is entered in a suspense account so that the totals agree temporarily and the financial statements can be drafted until the errors are found and corrected.
parts.working: 1 mark: totals disagree/difference recorded. 1 mark: temporary account until errors are found and corrected.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an error of principle.
parts.answer: An amount is entered in the correct amount and on the correct side, but in the wrong class of account, e.g. capital expenditure entered in an expense account.
parts.working: 1 mark: wrong class/type of account. 1 mark: example, e.g. purchase of a non-current asset debited to an expense account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether an error of principle will cause the trial balance totals to disagree. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No. The debit and the credit entries are still equal, so the totals agree.
parts.working: 1 mark: no. 1 mark: reason (equal debit and credit).

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text: A credit purchase of $2,100 from Bilal Traders was completely omitted from the books. Prepare the journal entry to correct this error. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer: Dr Purchases $2,100; Cr Bilal Traders $2,100

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this error did not cause the trial balance totals to disagree.
parts.answer: Neither the debit nor the credit was recorded, so both totals were understated by the same amount.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which error will cause the totals of a trial balance to disagree?
A a credit sale of $800 was omitted from the books completely
B the purchase of a computer for office use was debited to the purchases account
C discount allowed of $50 was entered in the discount allowed account but not in the customer's account
D a payment received from Ali was credited to Ahmed's account
parts.answer: C discount allowed of $50 was entered in the discount allowed account but not in the customer's account
parts.working: In C only one side of the double entry was made (a debit with no matching credit), so the trial balance will not agree. A (omission), B (principle) and D (commission) all have equal debits and credits, so the trial balance still agrees.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The purchase of an office printer costing $900 was debited to the purchases account. Depreciation is ignored. What is the effect of this error?
A gross profit and profit for the year are both understated by $900
B gross profit is understated by $900 but profit for the year is not affected
C gross profit and profit for the year are both overstated by $900
D profit for the year is not affected but non-current assets are overstated by $900
parts.answer: A gross profit and profit for the year are both understated by $900
parts.working: Purchases are overstated by $900, so cost of sales is $900 too high, and gross profit and therefore profit are both $900 too low. B is wrong because a lower gross profit carries through to profit. Non-current assets are understated, not overstated.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prepare journal entries to correct the following errors. Narratives are not required.
(i) Repairs to machinery, $640, were debited to the machinery account.
(ii) A credit sale of $1,230 to Lim Hardware was entered in the books as $1,320.
(iii) A payment of $500 by cheque to Patel Supplies was debited to the bank account and credited to Patel Supplies' account.
parts.answer:
(i) Dr Machinery repairs $640; Cr Machinery $640
(ii) Dr Sales $90; Cr Lim Hardware $90
(iii) Dr Patel Supplies $1,000; Cr Bank $1,000
parts.working: 2 marks per entry (1 debit, 1 credit with correct amount). (ii) difference 1,320 − 1,230 = 90. (iii) complete reversal is corrected with twice the amount: 2 × 500 = 1,000.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Shabnam's trial balance on 31 December had debit totals of $61,250 and credit totals of $61,650. The difference was entered in a suspense account. These errors were then found:
1 The purchases journal had been undercast by $280.
2 Rent paid of $1,150 had been entered in the rent account as $1,050.
3 Cash sales of $490 had been credited to the sales account as $510.
Prepare the suspense account, showing the opening balance and the corrections.
parts.answer: Suspense account: Dr balance b/d $400. Cr Purchases $280, Cr Rent $100, Cr Sales $20. Totals $400 each side.
parts.working: Opening balance: credits exceed debits by 61,650 − 61,250 = 400, so suspense has a debit balance of $400 (1). Purchases 280 on credit side (1). Rent 1,150 − 1,050 = 100 on credit side (1). Sales 510 − 490 = 20 on credit side (1); account closes with 280 + 100 + 20 = 400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one error that would not be corrected through the suspense account.
parts.answer: e.g. an error of omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal or compensating error (with example).

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each error state whether the profit for the year is overstated, understated or not affected, and by how much.
(i) Closing inventory was undervalued by $500.
(ii) Rent received of $300 was credited to the commission received account.
(iii) The purchase of shop fixtures, $750, was debited to the repairs account.
(iv) Wages owing of $420 at the year end were not recorded.
(v) A credit sale of $600 was omitted from the books.
parts.answer: (i) understated $500 (ii) not affected (iii) understated $750 (iv) overstated $420 (v) understated $600
parts.working: 1 mark each. (ii) both accounts are income accounts, so total income is unchanged. (iii) capital expenditure treated as an expense. (iv) an expense is missing.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Rosa's draft profit for the year ended 30 September was $31,560. The following errors were found:
1 Carriage outwards of $240, paid in cash, had not been recorded.
2 Discount allowed of $160 had been credited to the discount received account.
3 The purchase of office equipment, $1,200, had been debited to the office expenses account.
4 Closing inventory had been overstated by $700.
Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year. Depreciation is ignored.
parts.working: Draft 31560 − 240 (1) − 320 (1: income overstated 160 and expense understated 160) + 1,200 (1) − 700 (1) = 31500 (1 for final figure with correct method).

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a compensating error.
parts.answer: Two or more separate errors that cancel each other out, e.g. the sales account overcast by $100 and the wages account overcast by $100.
parts.working: 1 mark: two errors cancelling each other. 1 mark: example or statement that the trial balance still agrees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A credit sale of $745 to Kim was entered in the sales journal as $475 and posted from there. Prepare the journal entry to correct this error. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer: Dr Kim $270; Cr Sales $270

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of this type of error.
parts.answer: Error of original entry

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's draft profit for the year was $23,400. Two errors were then found:
1 discount received of $150 had been debited to the discount allowed account
2 closing inventory had been overstated by $1,200
What is the corrected profit for the year?
A $22,500
B $22,350
C $24,900
D $21,900
parts.working: Error 1: an expense (discount allowed) is overstated by $150 and income (discount received) is understated by $150, so profit is $300 too low: +300. Error 2: overstated closing inventory makes profit too high: −1,200. 23400 + 300 − 1,200 = 22500. B adjusts error 1 by only $150.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts
practice.stem:
Kofi's trial balance on 31 March did not agree: the debit side totalled $86,420 and the credit side $85,950. The difference was entered in a suspense account and a draft profit for the year of $18,600 was calculated. The following errors were then found:
1 The sales journal had been undercast by $300.
2 Wages of $1,240 had been entered in the wages account as $1,420.
3 Rent received of $250 had been entered in the bank account but omitted from the rent received account.
4 Discount allowed of $85 had not been posted to the discount allowed account.
5 A payment of $175 to Chen, a supplier, had been entered correctly in the cash book but not posted to Chen's account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the suspense account, starting with the balance arising from the trial balance.
parts.answer: Suspense: Cr balance b/d $470. Dr Sales $300, Dr Wages $180, Dr Rent received $250. Cr Discount allowed $85, Cr Chen $175. Totals $730 each side.
parts.working: Opening: debits exceed credits by 86420 − 85950 = 470, so a credit balance of 470 (1). Debit entries 300, 180 (1,420 − 1,240), 250 (1). Credit entries 85 and 175 (1). Both sides total 730.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Draft 18,600 + sales 300 (1) + wages 180 (1) + rent received 250 (1) − discount allowed 85 (1) = 19245. Error 5 affects only Chen's account and the suspense account, so there is no effect on profit.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts
practice.stem:
Bilal's draft financial statements for the year ended 31 December showed a profit of $27,400 and total current assets of $18,900. The following matters had not been dealt with:
1 Insurance of $360 had been paid in advance for next year.
2 A trade receivable of $520 was known to be irrecoverable and should be written off.
3 Closing inventory included goods that cost $900 but could only be sold for $650.
4 Commission of $430 was receivable but had not been received or recorded.
5 Cash drawings of $600 had been debited to the wages account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 27400 + 360 − 520 − 250 (900 − 650) + 430 + 600 = 28020. 1 mark for each two correct adjustments (max 3), 1 for the final figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected total current assets.
parts.working: 18900 + 360 prepayment − 520 receivable − 250 inventory + 430 commission receivable = 18920. Item 5 does not affect current assets. 2 marks for adjustments, 1 for the final figure.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts
practice.stem:
After a suspense account was opened, the following errors were found in Olena's books:
1 Discount received of $230 had not been posted to the discount received account.
2 The total of the sales returns journal, $410, had been posted to the credit of the sales returns account.
3 A cheque for $1,500 received from Fatima, a customer, had been entered correctly in the bank account but credited to Fatima's account as $1,050.
No other errors were found and correcting them closed the suspense account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entries to correct these errors. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
1 Dr Suspense $230; Cr Discount received $230
2 Dr Sales returns $820; Cr Suspense $820
3 Dr Suspense $450; Cr Fatima $450
parts.working: 2 marks each. Error 2: the amount was entered on the wrong side, so twice the amount (2 × 410 = 820) is needed. Error 3: 1,500 − 1,050 = 450.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance in the suspense account before the corrections were made and state whether it was a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: Debit balance of $140
parts.working: Corrections: debits to suspense 230 + 450 = 680; credit to suspense 820. For the account to close, the opening balance must be a debit of 820 − 680 = 140 (1 amount, 1 side).

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts
practice.stem:
Adebayo's draft income statement showed a gross profit of $42,800 and a profit for the year of $15,900. The following errors were then found:
1 Carriage inwards of $640 had been debited to the carriage outwards account.
2 Goods costing $1,100 taken by Adebayo for his own use had not been recorded.
3 Closing inventory had been undercast by $300.
4 Wages of $850 paid to a sales assistant had been debited to the purchases account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected gross profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 15900 + 1,100 + 300 = 17300. Errors 1 and 4 only move costs between cost of sales and expenses, so profit is unchanged (1 for this explanation, 1 each for the two adjustments).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why the balance in the cash book may differ from the balance on the bank statement on the same date.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. unpresented cheques; amounts paid in but not yet credited; bank charges or interest not yet entered in the cash book; standing orders or direct debits not yet recorded; credit transfers not yet recorded; dishonoured cheques; errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an unpresented cheque.
parts.answer: A cheque that has been written and entered in the cash book but has not yet been paid by the bank (not yet on the bank statement).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On 31 August the bank column of Yasmin's cash book showed a debit balance of $3,870. Her bank statement showed these items that were not in the cash book:
• bank charges, $45
• direct debit for insurance, $220
• credit transfer received from a customer, $680
• a cheque for $350 received from Ahmed had been dishonoured
State which of these items should be entered on the debit side of the cash book.
parts.answer: Only the credit transfer of $680.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the updated cash book balance on 31 August.
parts.answer: $3,935 debit
parts.working: 3,870 + 680 − 45 − 220 − 350 = 3935. 1 mark for adding 680, 1 for deducting the three payments, 1 for the final figure.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's updated cash book shows a debit balance of $2,340. Cheques paid to suppliers of $610 have not yet been presented, and a deposit of $450 has not yet been credited by the bank. What balance is shown on the bank statement?
A $2,500
B $2,180
C $3,400
D $1,280
parts.working: Unpresented cheques have not yet left the bank account, so the bank balance is higher: +610. The deposit is not yet on the statement, so the bank balance is lower: −450. 2340 + 610 − 450 = 2500. B reverses both adjustments.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After updating, the cash book of Hassan Electricals showed a debit balance of $5,612 on 30 June. The bank statement balance on the same date was $6,327. The difference was caused by:
• cheques paid to suppliers but not yet presented: $1,380 and $455
• cash paid in on 30 June but not yet credited by the bank: $1,120
Prepare a bank reconciliation statement on 30 June, starting with the balance on the bank statement.
parts.answer: Balance per bank statement $6,327; add amount not credited $1,120; less unpresented cheques $1,835; balance per cash book $5,612.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one item that would be entered in the cash book when it is updated but would not appear in the bank reconciliation statement.
parts.answer: e.g. bank charges, a standing order, a direct debit, a credit transfer, interest or a dishonoured cheque.

practice.stem:
On 31 October the bank column of Soo-jin's cash book showed an overdraft of $1,460. Comparison with the bank statement showed:
1 A standing order of $300 for rent had been paid by the bank but not entered in the cash book.
2 Bank interest of $85 had been charged.
3 A customer had paid $540 by credit transfer.
4 A cheque for $910 sent to a supplier had not been presented.
5 Takings of $1,275 paid in on 31 October had not been credited by the bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the updated cash book balance on 31 October. State whether it is a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: $1,305 credit (overdraft)
parts.working: −1,460 − 300 − 85 + 540 = -1305 (2 marks for adjustments), so an overdraft of 1305, a credit balance (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance shown on the bank statement on 31 October, stating whether it is an overdraft.
parts.answer: Overdraft of $1,670
parts.working: -1305 + 910 unpresented (1) − 1,275 not credited (1) = -1670, an overdraft of 1670 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the updated cash book balance will appear in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Under current liabilities (bank overdraft).

practice.stem:
On 31 May the bank statement of Dario's shop showed a balance of $8,140 in his favour. The following information is available:
• cheques of $2,350 entered in the cash book had not been presented
• a deposit of $1,600 had not been credited by the bank
• bank charges of $60 had not been entered in the cash book
• rent of $450 from a tenant had been received by credit transfer but not entered in the cash book

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the updated cash book balance on 31 May.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance shown in the cash book before it was updated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two benefits to Dario of preparing a bank reconciliation statement regularly.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. errors in the cash book or by the bank are found quickly; fraud is more likely to be detected; it shows which cheques are still unpresented or dishonoured; the cash book balance is brought up to date for the financial statements.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept vague answers such as 'finds errors' without saying where.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is entered on the credit side of a sales ledger control account?
A credit sales for the month
B cheques received from credit customers
C a customer's cheque that has been dishonoured
D the balance owed by customers brought down
parts.answer: B cheques received from credit customers
parts.working: Money received from credit customers reduces the amount they owe, so it is credited. Credit sales, dishonoured cheques and the opening debit balance all increase the amount owed and are debited.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two benefits of keeping control accounts.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. they check the arithmetical accuracy of the sales or purchases ledger; they help locate errors in a particular ledger; they give a quick total of trade receivables or payables; they help prevent fraud because the control account can be kept by a different person.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the source of information for (i) credit sales and (ii) discount allowed in a sales ledger control account.
parts.answer: (i) sales journal (ii) discount allowed column of the cash book

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prepare the sales ledger control account of Mirza Wholesale for March from the following information.
Balance owed by customers on 1 March $14,620
Credit sales $38,450
Sales returns $1,270
Cheques received from customers $35,900
Discount allowed $640
Irrecoverable debts written off $410
Customer's cheque dishonoured $300
Balance the account on 31 March and bring down the balance on 1 April.
parts.answer: Debit side: balance b/d 14,620, sales 38,450, bank (dishonoured cheque) 300 = 53,370. Credit side: sales returns 1,270, bank 35,900, discount allowed 640, irrecoverable debts 410, balance c/d 15,150. Balance b/d on 1 April $15,150 debit.
parts.working: 1 mark for the debit entries, 1 for returns and bank, 1 for discount and irrecoverable debts, 1 for balance c/d 15,150, 1 for balance b/d on the debit side.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The following information relates to the purchases ledger of Kaur Fabrics for April.
Balance owed to suppliers on 1 April $9,840
Credit purchases $27,300
Payments to suppliers $25,150
Discount received $520
Purchases returns $860
Amount set off against the sales ledger (contra) $700
Calculate the balance on the purchases ledger control account on 30 April and state whether it is a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: $9,910 credit

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a contra entry (set-off) between the control accounts.
parts.answer: When a business both buys from and sells to the same firm, the amount the firm owes is set off against the amount owed to it, so only the net amount is paid. It is debited in the purchases ledger control account and credited in the sales ledger control account.
parts.working: 1 mark: same person is both customer and supplier and balances are set off. 1 mark: correct entries (Dr PLCA, Cr SLCA).

practice.stem:
Yuki does not record credit sales in a sales journal. For the year ended 31 December she has the following information:
Trade receivables 1 January $12,300
Trade receivables 31 December $13,850
Cash and cheques received from credit customers $61,200
Discount allowed $1,150
Irrecoverable debts written off $600
Sales returns $2,050

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Yuki's credit sales for the year.
parts.working: Credit sales = closing 13,850 + receipts 61,200 + discount 1,150 + irrecoverable debts 600 + returns 2,050 − opening 12,300 = 66550. 3 marks for correct use of the items, 1 for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The total of the balances in Yuki's sales ledger on 31 December was $13,530. Suggest two reasons why this total differs from the control account balance.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. a customer's balance has been omitted from the list; an item was posted to the control account but not to a customer's account (or the reverse); a customer's account was miscast; an item was posted to the wrong side of a customer's account.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a sales ledger control account helps the owner to locate errors.
parts.answer: If the control account balance agrees with the total of the sales ledger balances, the ledger is probably arithmetically correct; if not, the error is in the sales ledger, so the search is limited to that ledger.
parts.working: 1 mark: comparison of control balance with list of balances. 1 mark: narrows the search to one ledger.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which balance appears on the credit side of a trial balance?
A drawings
B trade payables
C carriage inwards
D trade receivables
parts.answer: B trade payables
parts.working: Trade payables are a liability and have a credit balance. Drawings, carriage inwards (an expense) and trade receivables (an asset) have debit balances.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The following balances were taken from the books of Aryan Traders on 31 December.
Premises $60,000
Equipment $14,500
Inventory 1 January $8,200
Purchases $41,300
Revenue (sales) $72,900
Wages $15,600
Rent received $3,600
General expenses $4,450
Trade receivables $6,900
Trade payables $5,750
Bank overdraft $1,850
Loan (repayable 2032) $20,000
Drawings $9,000
Capital ?
Calculate the debit total of the trial balance and the capital balance that makes the trial balance agree.
parts.answer: Debit total $159,950; capital $55,850 (credit)
parts.working: Debits: premises, equipment, inventory, purchases, wages, general expenses, receivables, drawings = 159950 (2, 1 for correct classification). Credits without capital = 72,900 + 3,600 + 5,750 + 1,850 + 20,000 = 104100 (1). Capital = 159950 − 104100 = 55850 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of a trial balance.
parts.answer: Any two: it does not reveal errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal or compensating errors; it only proves arithmetical accuracy of the double entry; it does not show profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which transaction will increase a business's current ratio?
A buying a non-current asset and paying by bank transfer
B the owner withdrawing cash for private use
C receiving a long-term loan into the bank account
D receiving a cheque from a trade receivable
parts.answer: C receiving a long-term loan into the bank account
parts.working: A long-term loan increases bank (current asset) with no change in current liabilities, so the ratio rises. D only changes one current asset into another, so the ratio is unchanged.

practice.stem: A shoe retailer has a current ratio of 3.8 : 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a current ratio of 3.8 : 1 means.
parts.answer: Current assets are 3.8 times current liabilities

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a very high current ratio may not be good for the business.
parts.answer: Too much money tied up in idle assets (high inventory, high receivables or large bank balance) that could be invested to earn a return; may show poor inventory or credit control.

practice.stem: The rate of inventory turnover of a mobile phone shop fell from 9 times to 6 times a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a fall in the rate of inventory turnover means.
parts.answer: Inventory is being sold more slowly

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the business could improve its rate of inventory turnover.
parts.answer: Any two: hold lower inventory levels / buy smaller quantities more often; reduce selling prices or run promotions; advertise; stop buying slow-selling lines.

practice.stem: A furniture maker allows customers 30 days' credit. Its trade receivables turnover rose from 30 days to 52 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the change suggests about the customers.
parts.answer: Customers are taking longer to pay (beyond the 30-day credit terms)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible effects of this on the business.
parts.answer: Any two: less cash available / liquidity problems; may need an overdraft and pay interest; greater risk of irrecoverable debts; may pay its own suppliers late and lose discounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a business's gross margin may increase.
parts.answer: Any two: higher selling prices; cheaper purchases (better trade discounts, new supplier); change in sales mix to higher-margin goods; less inventory loss or theft.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit margin could fall even though the gross margin has increased.
parts.answer: Expenses (e.g. rent, wages, advertising) may have risen faster than gross profit, so a smaller share of revenue is left as profit.
parts.working: B1 expenses increased. B1 relative to revenue / gross profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shop's revenue increased but its gross margin fell. Which is the most likely reason?
A office rent increased
B selling prices were reduced to attract more customers
C more irrecoverable debts were written off
D wages of sales staff increased
parts.answer: B selling prices were reduced to attract more customers
parts.working: Lower selling prices reduce gross profit per $ of sales while increasing volume. A, C and D are expenses, which affect profit for the year but not gross margin.

practice.stem:
Zubair owns a building materials business. Ratios for two years:
Gross margin: 2025 38%, 2026 31%
Profit margin: 2025 14%, 2026 8%
Trade receivables turnover: 2025 35 days, 2026 58 days
Current ratio: 2025 1.9 : 1, 2026 1.1 : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Zubair should not be pleased with these results. Refer to three ratios.
parts.answer: Gross margin fell from 38% to 31%: less gross profit per $ of sales. Profit margin fell from 14% to 8%: expenses take a bigger share / profit per $ fell. Receivables collection rose from 35 to 58 days: customers pay more slowly, more risk of irrecoverable debts. Current ratio fell from 1.9 to 1.1: weaker ability to pay short-term debts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three ratios with a correct comment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways Zubair could improve the trade receivables collection period.
parts.answer: Any two: offer cash discounts for early payment; send statements and reminders promptly; set and enforce credit limits; charge interest on overdue accounts; check customers' creditworthiness.

practice.stem: Asma runs a bakery in Faisalabad and wants to buy a new oven costing $25,000. She can take a five-year bank loan at 9% interest per year, or use her personal savings, which earn 6% interest per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using a bank loan.
parts.answer: Advantage (any one): Asma keeps her savings for personal needs or emergencies; the cost is spread over five years; she still earns 6% on her savings. Disadvantage (any one): interest of 9% must be paid every year, reducing profit; repayments are needed even in poor years; the bank may require security.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Asma whether she should use the loan or her own savings to buy the oven. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Loan: interest 9% × 25,000 = 2,250 a year reduces profit; increases liabilities. Savings: no interest, but she loses the 6% (1,500 a year) savings interest and has less personal cash for emergencies. Using savings is cheaper by $750 a year; reasoned recommendation either way.
parts.working: B1 cost of loan. B1 opportunity cost of savings. B1 a further relevant point (risk, liquidity, control). B1 recommendation.

practice.stem: Rehan owns a growing phone accessories shop. His records are often weeks behind. A part-time book-keeper would cost $6,000 a year. His profit last year was $34,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two benefits of employing a part-time book-keeper.
parts.answer: Any two: records kept up to date and more accurate; frees Rehan's time to manage sales; better information for decisions; errors and fraud more likely to be found.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Rehan whether he should employ the book-keeper. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Cost $6,000 a year reduces profit; but late records may cause lost discounts, missed irrecoverable debts and poor decisions; recommendation with reason.
parts.working: B1 cost. B1 benefit linked to his situation. B1 recommendation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a business can make a profit but have a decreasing bank balance.
parts.answer: Profit includes credit sales not yet received and is after non-cash items; cash may be spent on non-current assets, loan repayments, drawings or extra inventory, which are not expenses.
parts.working: B1 timing / credit. B1 example of cash outflow not in profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Lubna's business made a profit of $22,000 but her bank balance fell by $5,000. Suggest two items that could explain this.
parts.answer: Any two: drawings; purchase of non-current assets; repayment of a loan; increase in trade receivables; increase in inventory; decrease in trade payables.

practice.stem: Mustafa's wholesale business pays its suppliers on average in 25 days but collects from its customers on average in 60 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this situation may cause problems for the business.
parts.answer: Cash leaves the business after 25 days but comes in only after 60 days, so it must finance 35 days of trade; it may run short of cash or need an overdraft.
parts.working: B1 comparison of the periods. B1 consequence for cash.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to increase the trade payables payment period without upsetting suppliers.
parts.answer: Negotiate longer credit terms with suppliers (or find suppliers offering longer credit)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of paying suppliers more slowly.
parts.answer: Loss of cash discounts / damaged reputation / suppliers may refuse credit

practice.stem:
Two branches of a stationery chain have the following at the year end:
Shop P: current assets $36,000 (including inventory $22,000); current liabilities $15,000
Shop Q: current assets $28,000 (including inventory $9,000); current liabilities $14,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and liquid ratio for each shop. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Shop P: current 2.40 : 1, liquid 0.93 : 1. Shop Q: current 2.00 : 1, liquid 1.36 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which shop has the stronger liquidity. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Shop Q: although its current ratio is lower, its liquid ratio is above 1 : 1 (1.36), so it can pay current liabilities without selling inventory; Shop P relies heavily on inventory (liquid ratio below 1).
parts.working: B1 Shop Q. B1 reason based on liquid ratio / inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has a current ratio of 2 : 1. Its current liabilities are $15,000 and its inventory is $12,000. What is its liquid (acid test) ratio?
A 0.8 : 1
B 1.2 : 1
C 1.8 : 1
D 2.8 : 1
parts.working: Current assets = 2 × 15,000 = 30,000; (30,000 − 12,000) ÷ 15,000 = 1.2 : 1. A divides inventory by current liabilities.

practice.stem: Saima sells kitchen appliances for cash only. Revenue is $180,000 a year with a gross margin of 30%. If she offers 30 days' credit, she expects extra sales of $60,000 a year at the same margin. She estimates irrecoverable debts at 2% of the extra sales and extra administration costs of $3,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected increase in profit for the year if Saima offers credit.
parts.working: Extra gross profit 60,000 × 30% = 18,000 (M1); less irrecoverable debts 1,200 and admin 3,000 (M1) = 13,800 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Saima whether she should start selling on credit. Justify your answer by giving two points for and two points against.
parts.answer: For: higher profit (13,800); attracts customers who want credit, competitors may offer it; larger orders from trade customers. Against: cash is received later, may need an overdraft; risk of irrecoverable debts may be higher than 2%; extra book-keeping and credit control work; estimates may not be achieved. Recommendation consistent with the points, e.g. offer credit with credit limits and checks.
parts.working: B1 each for two points for (max 2), B1 each for two points against (max 2), B1 recommendation.

practice.stem: Kamal runs a successful optician's shop in Rawalpindi and wants to open a second branch. Sara, an experienced marketing manager, offers to invest $40,000 and become a partner, sharing profits equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages and two disadvantages to Kamal of taking Sara into partnership.
parts.answer: Advantages (any two): extra capital $40,000 without borrowing; her marketing skills; shared workload and decisions; shared losses. Disadvantages (any two): profits shared; loss of sole control; possible disagreements; unlimited liability for partner's actions.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2 for and 2 against.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Kamal whether he should take Sara into partnership. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Recommendation with a reason that weighs the points, e.g. yes, because the extra capital lets him open the second shop, which may raise total profit enough that his share exceeds his current profit; a partnership agreement should be drawn up.

practice.stem: Nabeel's printing business made a profit of $18,600; he has no loans, so there is no interest. Capital employed is $155,000. He could sell the business for $155,000 and invest the money at 9% a year, and also take a job paying $12,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total income Nabeel could earn if he sold the business, invested the money and took the job.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Nabeel whether he should sell the business. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Financially the alternative gives $7,350 more than the business profit; but he would lose independence, the business may grow, investment returns and job may not be secure, and the business may not sell for $155,000. Reasoned recommendation.
parts.working: B1 financial comparison. B1 non-financial factor. B1 recommendation.

practice.stem: Aliya is a sole trader who runs a catering business. She plans a large expansion financed partly by friends who would invest but do not want to manage the business. She worries about losing her house if the expansion fails.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages to Aliya of converting the business into a private limited company.
parts.answer: Any two: limited liability for shareholders; easier to raise capital by issuing shares; separate legal entity / continuity; may improve status with suppliers and banks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of converting.
parts.answer: Any two: formation costs; accounts must follow legal requirements and may need audit; financial statements are less private; profits shared with other shareholders; some loss of control.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Aliya whether she should convert. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A clear decision that follows from the points, e.g. yes, because the expansion is risky and limited liability protects her house.

practice.stem: Bashir's furniture business normally has revenue of $200,000 and cost of sales of $140,000 a year (gross margin 30%). A hotel offers to buy furniture with a normal selling price of $40,000 if Bashir gives a 10% discount. Cost of sales for this furniture would be at the normal rate (70% of normal selling price).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit on the special order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new overall gross margin if the order is accepted. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Bashir whether he should accept the order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: gross profit rises by $8,000; uses spare capacity; possible repeat business. Against: margin falls; regular customers may demand the same discount; may need extra expenses or credit risk. Recommendation.
parts.working: B1 point for. B1 point against. B1 recommendation.

parts.text:
A business had revenue of $80,000 and gross profit of $24,000. What is the gross margin?
A 30%
B 42.86%
C 70%
D 24%

practice.stem: At 31 December 2025 Sadia's boutique had: inventory $14,600; trade receivables $9,800; bank $2,700; other receivables $400; trade payables $10,200; accrued expenses $800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the liquid (acid test) ratio. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why inventory is excluded from the liquid ratio.
parts.answer: Inventory is the least liquid current asset; it must be sold (and the money collected) before it becomes cash

practice.stem: A grocery shop adds a mark-up of 40% to cost. Its cost of sales for the year was $60,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shop's gross margin is 20%. What is its mark-up?
A 16.67%
B 20%
C 25%
D 80%
parts.working: Margin 20% means GP 20 on selling price 100, so cost 80; mark-up = 20 ÷ 80 = 25%. A confuses the conversion the other way round.

practice.stem: For the year ended 30 June 2026 an electrical goods wholesaler had credit sales of $146,000 and credit purchases of $109,500. At 30 June 2026 trade receivables were $16,000 and trade payables $13,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the trade receivables turnover in days (use a 365-day year).
parts.answer: 40 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the trade payables turnover in days (use a 365-day year).
parts.answer: 45 days

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the two results.
parts.answer: Customers pay in 40 days, but the business pays suppliers in 45 days, so it receives cash before it has to pay; good for cash flow, provided suppliers' credit terms are not exceeded.
parts.working: B1 comparison. B1 effect on liquidity / supplier terms.

practice.stem: A bicycle shop in Hanoi had revenue $125,000, cost of sales $81,250 and total expenses $30,000 for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the expenses as a percentage of revenue.

practice.stem: A hardware store had opening inventory of $12,400 and closing inventory of $15,800. Cost of sales for the year was $102,930.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average inventory.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inventory turnover in days (use a 365-day year).
parts.answer: 50 days

parts.label: c
parts.text: Last year the figure was 38 days. Suggest two possible reasons for the change.
parts.answer: Any two: sales have slowed; more inventory bought (e.g. bulk buying or before a price rise); slow-moving or obsolete items held; poor inventory control.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business had opening inventory $7,400, closing inventory $9,000 and cost of sales $98,400. What is the rate of inventory turnover?
A 10.93 times
B 12 times
C 13.30 times
D 8.2 times
parts.answer: B 12 times
parts.working: Average inventory (7,400 + 9,000) ÷ 2 = 8,200; 98,400 ÷ 8,200 = 12 times. A uses closing inventory only.

practice.stem: Yasir's capital on 1 January 2025 was $60,000. His profit for the year was $14,400, after charging loan interest of $1,600, and his drawings were $9,600. He has a long-term bank loan of $20,000. Capital employed = owner's capital at the end of the year + non-current liabilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Yasir's capital at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the capital employed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed (ROCE). Give your answer to two decimal places.

practice.stem: Information about Hina Traders for the year: opening inventory $11,000; closing inventory $13,000; rate of inventory turnover 8 times (based on average inventory); gross margin 25%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revenue.
parts.working: Cost of sales is 75% of revenue: 96,000 ÷ 0.75 (M1) = 128,000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A supplier is deciding whether to give 60 days' credit to a new customer. Which ratio will the supplier find most useful?
A gross margin
B return on capital employed
C liquid (acid test) ratio
D rate of inventory turnover
parts.answer: C liquid (acid test) ratio
parts.working: The supplier wants to know if the customer can pay short-term debts, which the liquid ratio shows. ROCE (B) measures profitability, which is more relevant to owners and investors.

practice.stem: Imtiaz owns a pharmacy in Hyderabad and wants to compare its ratios with those of a pharmacy owned by his cousin in Karachi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two users of a sole trader's financial statements, other than the owner, and state what each would want to know.
parts.answer: Any two, with a matching interest: bank/lender (ability to repay loan and interest); trade payables (ability to pay on time); employees (job security, ability to pay wages); tax authorities (profit for tax); potential buyer or partner (profitability).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three limitations of comparing the ratios of two businesses.
parts.answer: Any three: different accounting policies (e.g. depreciation methods, inventory valuation); different sizes or locations; financial statements are historical; figures may be at different dates or for different periods; non-financial factors (staff, reputation) are ignored; one business may own premises and the other rent.

practice.subtopic: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A customer who owes Shazia $480 has left the country and the debt will not be paid. Which entries record writing off the debt?
A Debit irrecoverable debts, credit the customer's account
B Debit the customer's account, credit irrecoverable debts
C Debit provision for doubtful debts, credit irrecoverable debts
D Debit irrecoverable debts, credit sales
parts.answer: A Debit irrecoverable debts, credit the customer's account
parts.working: The expense (irrecoverable debts) is debited and the asset (the customer's account) is reduced by a credit. B is the reverse entry, used only when a written-off debt is reinstated.

practice.subtopic: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an irrecoverable debt and a doubtful debt.
parts.answer: Irrecoverable debt: certain not to be paid, so written off. Doubtful debt: may not be paid, so a provision is made but the debt stays in the customer's account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why a business creates a provision for doubtful debts.
parts.answer: Any two: prudence (not overstating assets/profit); matching the expected loss with the revenue of the year it arose; showing a realistic value of trade receivables; spreading the effect of bad debts.

practice.subtopic: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts
practice.stem: Rizwan Stores owed a supplier $2,000 and was declared bankrupt. The supplier received a final payment of 30 cents for every $1 owed. The rest is irrecoverable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be written off as irrecoverable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the entries in the supplier's books for the cash received and the amount written off.
parts.answer: Debit bank $600, credit Rizwan Stores $600; debit irrecoverable debts $1,400, credit Rizwan Stores $1,400.

practice.subtopic: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At 31 December 2025 a business had trade receivables of $48,000. It keeps a provision for doubtful debts of 3% of trade receivables. The provision brought forward was $1,200. What is the effect on the income statement for 2025?
A expense of $240
B income of $240
C expense of $1,440
D expense of $2,640
parts.answer: A expense of $240
parts.working: New provision 3% × 48,000 = 1,440; increase 1,440 − 1,200 = 240, charged as an expense. C wrongly charges the whole provision.

practice.subtopic: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts
practice.stem: Before adjustments, a furniture wholesaler had trade receivables of $62,500 on 30 June 2026. A debt of $2,500 is to be written off. The provision for doubtful debts is to be kept at 4% of the remaining trade receivables. The provision on 1 July 2025 was $2,100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for doubtful debts required at 30 June 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the provision and state whether it is income or an expense in the income statement.
parts.answer: Increase of $300; expense

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net trade receivables shown in the statement of financial position.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the accounting principle applied when making the provision.
parts.answer: Prudence

practice.subtopic: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts
practice.stem: A printing firm in Colombo created a provision for doubtful debts on 31 December 2024 of 5% of trade receivables, which were $30,000. On 31 December 2025 trade receivables were $26,000 and the rate stayed at 5%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount charged to the income statement for the year ended 31 December 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the provision required at 31 December 2025 and the amount shown in the income statement for 2025, stating whether it is income or an expense.
parts.answer: Provision $1,300; decrease of $200 shown as income

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the balance on the provision for doubtful debts account brought down on 1 January 2026 and its side.
parts.answer: $1,300 credit

practice.subtopic: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts
practice.stem: In the year ended 31 March 2025 Kamila wrote off a debt of $650 owed by Wahid. In January 2026 Wahid paid the full $650 by cheque.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two entries needed to reinstate the debt.
parts.answer: Debit Wahid's account $650; credit irrecoverable debts recovered $650
parts.working: B1 debit customer. B1 credit irrecoverable debts recovered (income).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the entries to record the receipt of the cheque.
parts.answer: Debit bank $650; credit Wahid's account $650

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the debt is reinstated in Wahid's account before the receipt is recorded.
parts.answer: So that the customer's account shows a full record of his payment history, which helps when deciding whether to give him credit again.
parts.working: B1 complete record. B1 used for future credit decisions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the effect of the recovery on the profit for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: Profit increases by $650

practice.subtopic: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts
practice.stem: Tahir's draft profit for the year ended 30 September 2026 was $41,800. Trade receivables at that date were $35,900, before writing off a debt of $900. The provision for doubtful debts, previously $1,050, is to be 2.5% of the remaining trade receivables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new provision for doubtful debts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

practice.subtopic: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts
practice.stem:
A wholesaler of solar panels in Lagos bases its provision for doubtful debts on the age of each debt. At 31 December 2025:
Debts up to 30 days old: $18,000 (provision 1%)
Debts 31–60 days old: $7,500 (provision 4%)
Debts over 60 days old: $2,400 (provision 10%)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for doubtful debts required at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The provision on 1 January 2025 was $900. State the amount and effect on the profit for 2025.
parts.answer: Decrease of $180; profit increases by $180

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways the business could reduce its irrecoverable debts in future.
parts.answer: Any two: check credit references before giving credit; set credit limits; offer cash discounts for early payment; send statements and reminders promptly; stop supplying customers who pay late.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bakery bought an oven for $24,000. It is expected to last 5 years and then be sold for $4,000. What is the annual depreciation charge using the straight-line method?
A $4,000

practice.subtopic: Depreciation and disposal of non-current assets

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define depreciation.
parts.answer: The loss in value (cost spread over the useful life) of a non-current asset

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three causes of depreciation.
parts.answer: Any three: wear and tear; passage of time; obsolescence (new technology); depletion; using up of the asset.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the accounting principle applied when depreciation is charged in each year an asset is used.
parts.answer: Matching (accruals)

practice.subtopic: Depreciation and disposal of non-current assets
practice.stem: A car repair workshop values its loose tools each year. On 1 April 2025 the tools were valued at $2,600. During the year tools costing $900 were bought. On 31 March 2026 the tools were valued at $2,850.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation of loose tools for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the revaluation method is suitable for loose tools.
parts.answer: They are many low-cost items that are easily lost or broken, so recording each one separately would be impractical.

practice.subtopic: Depreciation and disposal of non-current assets
practice.stem: Rashid & Co sold a delivery vehicle for $5,900 by cheque. The vehicle had cost $18,000 and accumulated depreciation on it was $11,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net book value of the vehicle at the date of sale.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on disposal.
parts.answer: Loss $900

parts.label: c
parts.text: List the entries in the disposal account.
parts.answer: Debit: motor vehicles (cost) $18,000. Credit: provision for depreciation $11,200; bank $5,900; income statement (loss) $900.
parts.working: B1 cost debited. B1 accumulated depreciation and proceeds credited. B1 loss credited (to balance).

practice.subtopic: Depreciation and disposal of non-current assets
practice.stem: On 1 January 2025 a laboratory in Karachi had equipment at cost of $40,000. On 1 July 2025 it bought more equipment for $12,000. Depreciation is 10% per annum on cost, calculated monthly from the date of purchase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge on equipment for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the equipment is shown in the statement of financial position, if accumulated depreciation at 31 December 2025 is $19,600.
parts.answer: Under non-current assets: cost $52,000 less accumulated depreciation $19,600 = net book value $32,400.

practice.subtopic: Depreciation and disposal of non-current assets

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A machine was bought on 1 January 2023 for $15,000. It is depreciated at 20% per annum using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2025?
A $1,920
